The $n$-queens problem asks to place $n$ queens on an $n \times n$ chessboard such that no two queens attack each other.
This means no two queens can share the same row, column, or diagonal.
Since we need to place 26 queens on a 26x26 board, and no two queens can share a row, there must be exactly one queen in each row.
Similarly, no two queens can share a column, so there must be exactly one queen in each column.
The solution can be represented as a permutation $p$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, 25\}$, where $p[i]$ is the column index of the queen in row $i$.
The condition that no two queens share a diagonal means that for any distinct $i, j$, $|i - j| \neq |p[i] - p[j]|$.
